analysis.one_liner: Taxes lead production to fund removing lead paint hazards from homes.
analysis.headline: A bill to tax lead and use the money to remove lead-paint hazards in housing died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Bill Bradley proposed a 45-cent-per-pound tax on lead taken from U.S. smelters and on lead in imported products. The money would go into a dedicated federal trust fund, and states and local governments could draw grants from it to find and remove lead-based paint hazards in homes, following the framework Congress passed in the 1992 housing law. Exporters would get the tax refunded, and the tax would stop automatically if the fund already held more than $2.5 billion it hadn't spent.
analysis.who_benefits: Families living in older housing with lead-based paint, especially young children, who face the greatest harm from lead exposure. States and cities would get a dedicated funding stream for inspection and abatement work, and the contractors doing that work would gain business.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated trust fund, financed by the lead tax, whose money can only be spent on grants to evaluate and reduce lead-based paint hazards [S2] [S3].
Authorizes spending from the fund under title X of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1992, the existing federal framework for lead hazard reduction [S3].
Lead exposure in children is linked to lasting developmental harm, so removing paint hazards targets one of the most preventable environmental health threats to kids [S2].

analysis.who_pays: U.S. lead smelters pay the tax on lead they produce, and importers pay it on lead and lead-containing products brought into the country; both would likely pass some of the cost to buyers of lead products such as batteries [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The 45-cent-per-pound tax raises the cost of domestic and imported lead, and smelters and importers pass some of that cost through to buyers of lead products like batteries [S2] [S3].
The abatement money would flow only as Congress approves it year by year through appropriations, not automatically, so the fund could sit unspent [S3].
The bill included no study of how much revenue the tax would raise or how it compares to the scale of the national lead hazard problem, leaving the adequacy of the funding unanswered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is narrowly aimed at lead itself, and exporters get refunds, so the cost is concentrated on domestic lead production and imports rather than spread broadly. Against that is a dedicated funding stream for removing a hazard that permanently harms children's development. The main weaknesses are the modest, unexamined revenue base and the appropriations gate, not the design of the tax itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 1995 without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bradley introduced the bill on August 3, 1993, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S5] [S1].
No cosponsors ever joined the bill [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill received no floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lead smelters and importers never faced the tax, and no federal abatement fund was created; families in lead-paint housing stayed exposed to the hazard.

for.name: Bill Bradley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: The committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or acted on the bill after it was referred, letting it die at the end of the Congress [S5] [S1].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsor signed on, so the partisan split was never tested; the single sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.note: They would have paid a 45-cent-per-pound tax on every pound of lead produced or imported, which is exactly the money that would have funded lead hazard removal. Avoiding the tax meant no dedicated abatement fund.

industries.industry: Lead product manufacturers (batteries and other goods)
industries.note: They would bear some of the tax passed through on lead inputs, though exporters of lead products would get the tax refunded [S3].
Grants from the trust fund would pay for the testing and removal work they perform, expanding demand for their services alongside the public health benefit.
